Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 with 2 replicas using image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29. It matches the stable deployment’s container settings (container name rec-engine, containerPort 80) and security configuration (no special pod/container securityContext).
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version selector), keeping port 80 -> targetPort 8080. This targets both the stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods.
- With 2 replicas on each Deployment (engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1), the Service will distribute traffic roughly 50/50 across pods.

Current status:
- Pods: 4 total running (2x engine-v2-0 [v2.0], 2x engine-v2-1 [v2.1]) and ready.

Notes and adjustments:
- To shift weight, change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To revert to 100% stable quickly, either scale engine-v2-1 to 0 or set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

Done. The Deployment was failing because it overrode the container command to run “/bin/sh -c nonexistent_command”, causing a CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed:
- Removed the invalid command/args so the nginx-unprivileged image starts normally.
- Kept the image as quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and exposed its default port 8080 in the pod spec.

Current state:
- Pod crashloop-test/app-b6f9d445-mvm5f is Running (1/1) with 0 restarts.
- Previous Warning events show the old back-off, but the new ReplicaSet pod is healthy.

If you want, I can also:
- Expose it via a Service (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer) or create an Ingress/Route.
- Add liveness/readiness probes on port 8080.

results.taskOutput:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc couldn’t bind: storageclass "sc" not found.
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (storageClassName was sc, which doesn’t exist).
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass available in your cluster).

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (SC: standard, 1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, 1/1 containers Ready.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.22
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster

Notes
- Because the original PVC was never bound, deleting and recreating it didn’t risk data loss.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want me to create a StorageClass named sc, I can switch it for you.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I found the root cause and fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc couldn’t bind: storageclass "sc" not found.
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (storageClassName was sc, which doesn’t exist).
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass available in your cluster).

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (SC: standard, 1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, 1/1 containers Ready.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.22
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster

Notes
- Because the original PVC was never bound, deleting and recreating it didn’t risk data loss.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want me to create a StorageClass named sc, I can switch it for you.

outputSteps.content:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc couldn’t bind: storageclass "sc" not found.
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (storageClassName was sc, which doesn’t exist).
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass available in your cluster).

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (SC: standard, 1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, 1/1 containers Ready.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.22
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster

Notes
- Because the original PVC was never bound, deleting and recreating it didn’t risk data loss.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want me to create a StorageClass named sc, I can switch it for you.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The nginx image in your Deployment listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were checking HTTP on port 80 and on non-existent paths (/is_ready, /get_status), causing constant probe failures.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so it had no ready endpoints and the app was unreachable.

What I changed (orders namespace)
- Deployment webapp:
  - Expose container port 8080 (named it http).
  - Set readiness and liveness probes to GET / on port http (8080).
- Service webapp:
  - Target port changed to http (8080). Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Pod webapp-847d7c6654-hnkxx is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.25:8080.
- Health checks return 200 OK. The previous unhealthy pod is being rolled down by the Deployment controller.

How to access
- Inside the cluster: use Service webapp on port 80 (ClusterIP 10.100.147.48), e.g., http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/.

Want it externally accessible?
- I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service if you tell me the hostname or exposure method you prefer.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The nginx image in your Deployment listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were checking HTTP on port 80 and on non-existent paths (/is_ready, /get_status), causing constant probe failures.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so it had no ready endpoints and the app was unreachable.

What I changed (orders namespace)
- Deployment webapp:
  - Expose container port 8080 (named it http).
  - Set readiness and liveness probes to GET / on port http (8080).
- Service webapp:
  - Target port changed to http (8080). Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Pod webapp-847d7c6654-hnkxx is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.25:8080.
- Health checks return 200 OK. The previous unhealthy pod is being rolled down by the Deployment controller.

How to access
- Inside the cluster: use Service webapp on port 80 (ClusterIP 10.100.147.48), e.g., http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/.

Want it externally accessible?
- I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service if you tell me the hostname or exposure method you prefer.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The nginx image in your Deployment listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were checking HTTP on port 80 and on non-existent paths (/is_ready, /get_status), causing constant probe failures.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so it had no ready endpoints and the app was unreachable.

What I changed (orders namespace)
- Deployment webapp:
  - Expose container port 8080 (named it http).
  - Set readiness and liveness probes to GET / on port http (8080).
- Service webapp:
  - Target port changed to http (8080). Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Pod webapp-847d7c6654-hnkxx is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.25:8080.
- Health checks return 200 OK. The previous unhealthy pod is being rolled down by the Deployment controller.

How to access
- Inside the cluster: use Service webapp on port 80 (ClusterIP 10.100.147.48), e.g., http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/.

Want it externally accessible?
- I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service if you tell me the hostname or exposure method you prefer.

Root cause

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing apps/deployments and didn’t grant any permissions on core/v1 pods. So the pod-reader ServiceAccount had no rights to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup to include read-only access to pods:
  - apiGroup: "" (core), resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - Kept existing permission to list apps/deployments

Why it works now
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already binds ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to Role/pod-reader-role in the same namespace, so adding pods permissions to that Role immediately enables pod listing for that ServiceAccount in simple-rbac-setup.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

If you ever need to list pods across multiple namespaces, you’d need a ClusterRole with the same rules and a ClusterRoleBinding (or per-namespace Role/RoleBinding).

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service web/nginx had selector app=web
  - Pods from the Deployment are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty, so the Service had no backends
- Port mismatch:
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service was targeting port 80
  - Even once pods were selected, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach nginx

Fix applied
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and target the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- The Service remains type: ClusterIP (internal-only)

Current state and verification
- Endpoints now populated:
  - web/nginx -> 10.244.0.26:8080
- In-cluster access works:
  - From a test pod in web: curl http://nginx returns the nginx welcome page with HTTP 200
  - DNS for nginx.web.svc.cluster.local resolves to the Service ClusterIP

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it is not reachable from outside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort Service (simple, exposes on each node)
  - LoadBalancer Service (cloud provider or MetalLB)
  - Ingress (with an Ingress controller; we can configure a host/path)

If you want, I can:
- Delete the test pod curl-test I used for verification
- Expose nginx externally via NodePort/LoadBalancer or set up an Ingress (tell me which you prefer)

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service web/nginx had selector app=web
  - Pods from the Deployment are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty, so the Service had no backends
- Port mismatch:
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service was targeting port 80
  - Even once pods were selected, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach nginx

Fix applied
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and target the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- The Service remains type: ClusterIP (internal-only)

Current state and verification
- Endpoints now populated:
  - web/nginx -> 10.244.0.26:8080
- In-cluster access works:
  - From a test pod in web: curl http://nginx returns the nginx welcome page with HTTP 200
  - DNS for nginx.web.svc.cluster.local resolves to the Service ClusterIP

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it is not reachable from outside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort Service (simple, exposes on each node)
  - LoadBalancer Service (cloud provider or MetalLB)
  - Ingress (with an Ingress controller; we can configure a host/path)

If you want, I can:
- Delete the test pod curl-test I used for verification
- Expose nginx externally via NodePort/LoadBalancer or set up an Ingress (tell me which you prefer)

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service web/nginx had selector app=web
  - Pods from the Deployment are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty, so the Service had no backends
- Port mismatch:
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service was targeting port 80
  - Even once pods were selected, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach nginx

Fix applied
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and target the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- The Service remains type: ClusterIP (internal-only)

Current state and verification
- Endpoints now populated:
  - web/nginx -> 10.244.0.26:8080
- In-cluster access works:
  - From a test pod in web: curl http://nginx returns the nginx welcome page with HTTP 200
  - DNS for nginx.web.svc.cluster.local resolves to the Service ClusterIP

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it is not reachable from outside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort Service (simple, exposes on each node)
  - LoadBalancer Service (cloud provider or MetalLB)
  - Ingress (with an Ingress controller; we can configure a host/path)

If you want, I can:
- Delete the test pod curl-test I used for verification
- Expose nginx externally via NodePort/LoadBalancer or set up an Ingress (tell me which you prefer)

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a hard nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu. The only node has no such label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods.
- Evidence:
  - Pod events: FailedScheduling: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints (EndpointSlice showed none), so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment and redeployed it (delete + re-create to ensure the selector was cleared).
- Result:
  - Pods are now running:
    - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-5qwx9 – Running, IP 10.244.0.30
    - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-v5wxw – Running, IP 10.244.0.31
  - Service endpoints are populated on port 80:
    - EndpointSlice web-app-service-zgkcp -> 10.244.0.30, 10.244.0.31:80

Why this fixes the error
- With pods now scheduled and ready, the ClusterIP service has active endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed instead of being refused.

How you can validate
- From any pod in the cluster (e.g., your frontend pod):
  - kubectl exec -n webshop-frontend <frontend-pod> -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service
  - or curl http://web-app-service
- Check service endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpointslice -n webshop-frontend | grep web-app-service

Notes and follow-ups
- If you actually need to constrain this workload to special nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the correct node(s): kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment
  - Or use a preferredDuringScheduling (soft) nodeAffinity so it still schedules if none are available.
- Consider:
  - Adding a readinessProbe for Nginx on port 80 so traffic only routes when ready.
  - Pinning image tag instead of latest.
  - Setting resource requests/limits.

Tell me if you want me to add readiness probes and resource limits now, or to reintroduce node placement with the correct labels/affinity.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a hard nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu. The only node has no such label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods.
- Evidence:
  - Pod events: FailedScheduling: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints (EndpointSlice showed none), so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment and redeployed it (delete + re-create to ensure the selector was cleared).
- Result:
  - Pods are now running:
    - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-5qwx9 – Running, IP 10.244.0.30
    - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-v5wxw – Running, IP 10.244.0.31
  - Service endpoints are populated on port 80:
    - EndpointSlice web-app-service-zgkcp -> 10.244.0.30, 10.244.0.31:80

Why this fixes the error
- With pods now scheduled and ready, the ClusterIP service has active endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed instead of being refused.

How you can validate
- From any pod in the cluster (e.g., your frontend pod):
  - kubectl exec -n webshop-frontend <frontend-pod> -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service
  - or curl http://web-app-service
- Check service endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpointslice -n webshop-frontend | grep web-app-service

Notes and follow-ups
- If you actually need to constrain this workload to special nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the correct node(s): kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment
  - Or use a preferredDuringScheduling (soft) nodeAffinity so it still schedules if none are available.
- Consider:
  - Adding a readinessProbe for Nginx on port 80 so traffic only routes when ready.
  - Pinning image tag instead of latest.
  - Setting resource requests/limits.

Tell me if you want me to add readiness probes and resource limits now, or to reintroduce node placement with the correct labels/affinity.

Diagnosis
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a hard nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu. The only node has no such label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods.
- Evidence:
  - Pod events: FailedScheduling: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints (EndpointSlice showed none), so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment and redeployed it (delete + re-create to ensure the selector was cleared).
- Result:
  - Pods are now running:
    - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-5qwx9 – Running, IP 10.244.0.30
    - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-v5wxw – Running, IP 10.244.0.31
  - Service endpoints are populated on port 80:
    - EndpointSlice web-app-service-zgkcp -> 10.244.0.30, 10.244.0.31:80

Why this fixes the error
- With pods now scheduled and ready, the ClusterIP service has active endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed instead of being refused.

How you can validate
- From any pod in the cluster (e.g., your frontend pod):
  - kubectl exec -n webshop-frontend <frontend-pod> -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service
  - or curl http://web-app-service
- Check service endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpointslice -n webshop-frontend | grep web-app-service

Notes and follow-ups
- If you actually need to constrain this workload to special nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the correct node(s): kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment
  - Or use a preferredDuringScheduling (soft) nodeAffinity so it still schedules if none are available.
- Consider:
  - Adding a readinessProbe for Nginx on port 80 so traffic only routes when ready.
  - Pinning image tag instead of latest.
  - Setting resource requests/limits.

All requested namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network/network isolation policies have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Namespaces labeled for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, role=developer, tenant=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts per developer:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace (least-privilege “edit” role):
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace bind:
    - User alice→dev-alice, SA alice-sa→dev-alice
    - User bob→dev-bob, SA bob-sa→dev-bob
    - User charlie→dev-charlie, SA charlie-sa→dev-charlie
  - Uses ClusterRole edit (write on namespaced resources, not RBAC)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings were created; access limited to cluster admins by default RBAC

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six non-system namespaces
- DNS/system services access:
  - Egress allowed to kube-system TCP/UDP 53 in each namespace (CoreDNS)
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only
  - No ingress from other namespaces (prevents cross-developer access and dev-shared→dev-ns ingress)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress
  - Allow ingress from developer namespaces (env=dev, role=developer)
  - Egress policy present toward developer namespaces, but blocked by dev-ns default-deny ingress (so effective direction is dev-ns→dev-shared)
- staging/prod:
  - Default deny + same-namespace only + DNS egress
  - No dev namespace communication (complete isolation from dev)

Notes on least privilege and isolation
- Developers have write access only in their own namespaces and read-only rights in dev-shared; they have no permissions in staging/prod.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave Net).
- System namespaces were not modified; default-deny was not applied there.

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding dev-alice-edit-binding -o yaml
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding developers-view-binding -o yaml
- Quotas:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota rq-compute -o yaml
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get resourcequota rq-compute -o yaml
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get networkpolicy
  - Optional connectivity test (from a test pod in dev-alice):
    - Same-namespace allowed (service/pod in dev-alice) → should succeed
    - To dev-shared service → should succeed
    - To dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod → should fail
    - DNS resolution (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) → should succeed

If you want default resource requests/limits per Pod, I can add LimitRanges for each namespace.

  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace (least-privilege “edit” role):
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace bind:
    - User alice→dev-alice, SA alice-sa→dev-alice
    - User bob→dev-bob, SA bob-sa→dev-bob
    - User charlie→dev-charlie, SA charlie-sa→dev-charlie
  - Uses ClusterRole edit (write on namespaced resources, not RBAC)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings were created; access limited to cluster admins by default RBAC

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six non-system namespaces
- DNS/system services access:
  - Egress allowed to kube-system TCP/UDP 53 in each namespace (CoreDNS)
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only
  - No ingress from other namespaces (prevents cross-developer access and dev-shared→dev-ns ingress)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress
  - Allow ingress from developer namespaces (env=dev, role=developer)
  - Egress policy present toward developer namespaces, but blocked by dev-ns default-deny ingress (so effective direction is dev-ns→dev-shared)
- staging/prod:
  - Default deny + same-namespace only + DNS egress
  - No dev namespace communication (complete isolation from dev)

Notes on least privilege and isolation
- Developers have write access only in their own namespaces and read-only rights in dev-shared; they have no permissions in staging/prod.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave Net).
- System namespaces were not modified; default-deny was not applied there.

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding dev-alice-edit-binding -o yaml
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding developers-view-binding -o yaml
- Quotas:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota rq-compute -o yaml
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get resourcequota rq-compute -o yaml
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get networkpolicy
  - Optional connectivity test (from a test pod in dev-alice):
    - Same-namespace allowed (service/pod in dev-alice) → should succeed
    - To dev-shared service → should succeed
    - To dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod → should fail
    - DNS resolution (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) → should succeed

If you want default resource requests/limits per Pod, I can add LimitRanges for each namespace.

outputSteps.content:
All requested namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network/network isolation policies have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Namespaces labeled for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, role=developer, tenant=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts per developer:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace (least-privilege “edit” role):
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace bind:
    - User alice→dev-alice, SA alice-sa→dev-alice
    - User bob→dev-bob, SA bob-sa→dev-bob
    - User charlie→dev-charlie, SA charlie-sa→dev-charlie
  - Uses ClusterRole edit (write on namespaced resources, not RBAC)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings were created; access limited to cluster admins by default RBAC

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six non-system namespaces
- DNS/system services access:
  - Egress allowed to kube-system TCP/UDP 53 in each namespace (CoreDNS)
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only
  - No ingress from other namespaces (prevents cross-developer access and dev-shared→dev-ns ingress)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress
  - Allow ingress from developer namespaces (env=dev, role=developer)
  - Egress policy present toward developer namespaces, but blocked by dev-ns default-deny ingress (so effective direction is dev-ns→dev-shared)
- staging/prod:
  - Default deny + same-namespace only + DNS egress
  - No dev namespace communication (complete isolation from dev)

Notes on least privilege and isolation
- Developers have write access only in their own namespaces and read-only rights in dev-shared; they have no permissions in staging/prod.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave Net).
- System namespaces were not modified; default-deny was not applied there.

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding dev-alice-edit-binding -o yaml
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding developers-view-binding -o yaml
- Quotas:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota rq-compute -o yaml
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get resourcequota rq-compute -o yaml
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get networkpolicy
  - Optional connectivity test (from a test pod in dev-alice):
    - Same-namespace allowed (service/pod in dev-alice) → should succeed
    - To dev-shared service → should succeed
    - To dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod → should fail
    - DNS resolution (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) → should succeed

If you want default resource requests/limits per Pod, I can add LimitRanges for each namespace.

  - data-db-0: Bound, 1Gi, StorageClass: standard
